questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Custody and the requirement of warnings
questions.learningObjective: Identify when a police encounter triggers the duty to give warnings
questions.stem: In your logbook for the Pine Ridge Observatory you note that a stopped motorist was held in the patrol car long enough for officers to ask questions. Which observation best matches the custody that requires warnings before questioning?

options.text: The driver was physically restrained by officers, so warnings were required before any questioning
The driver was free to walk away at any moment, so no warnings were needed even if the exchange felt tense
options.misconception: assumes a stopped driver is never in custody

options.text: Custody begins only on a formal arrest, so a roadside stop never requires any warning
options.misconception: thinks formal arrest is required for custody

options.text: Warnings were required only after the driver was formally charged with an offence
options.misconception: believes warnings depend on a formal charge

questions.explanation: Custody turns on whether a reasonable person would feel free to leave, and officer restraint satisfies that. Warnings are required for custodial interrogation regardless of arrest or charge.
questions.hint: Ask whether a reasonable person could walk away.

questions.topic: Testimonial and nontestimonial acts
questions.learningObjective: Classify police procedures as testimonial or nontestimonial
questions.stem: Your notebook lists four items taken during a summer observing shift: a suspect wrote a specimen phrase for handwriting comparison, a witness identified the suspect in a lineup, an officer asked where the missing cash was hidden, and a driver gave a blood sample. Which recorded act is testimonial?

options.text: Writing the specimen phrase, because written words are always testimonial
options.misconception: assumes any writing counts as testimonial

options.text: The exchange about where the cash was hidden, because the answer was made to communicate with the officer
The blood sample, because the body was used to produce evidence
options.misconception: treats a physical sample as communication

options.text: The lineup identification, because it involved speech about the suspect
options.misconception: assumes any speech in a lineup is testimonial

questions.explanation: A testimonial act communicates with police for the purpose of conveying information. Specimens, blood draws and lineup identifications are physical acts whose object is the evidence itself.
questions.hint: Focus on communication aimed at the officer.

questions.topic: The grand jury requirement for serious charges
questions.learningObjective: Locate the secret and one-sided stage of a serious charge
questions.stem: Your notebook sketches this flow: felony complaint filed, prosecutor decides to seek an indictment, grand jury hears witnesses in secret, the panel votes, an information is filed, trial follows. At which step is defence counsel absent by design?

options.text: At the complaint step, because defence counsel cannot appear before a charging document exists
options.misconception: thinks counsel is barred from the complaint stage

options.text: At the information step, because the defendant has not yet been arraigned
options.misconception: links counsel rights to arraignment only

options.text: At the trial step, because a jury must be chosen without the defendant present
options.misconception: confuses jury selection with the charging stage

options.text: At the grand jury step, because the hearing is secret and one-sided by design

questions.explanation: The grand jury hears evidence in secret without the defendant or counsel, and it is not bound by the rules of evidence. Its vote, not the judge's view, decides whether a felony indictment issues.
questions.hint: Which body meets without the defendant present?

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Two offences and the same-elements test
questions.learningObjective: Explain how courts decide whether two charges are one offence
questions.stem: While reviewing a friend's observing log you find a note that one incident produced two separate convictions for the same behaviour. Explain, in your own words, how a court decides whether the two charges describe one offence or two, and what follows if they are two.

answer.exemplar: A court asks whether each offence requires proof of the same elements, or whether one is a lesser included offence of the other. If the charges are the same offence, cumulative punishment for both would violate the guarantee against double punishment; if they are distinct, separate punishment is permitted.

questions.explanation: The same-elements test compares what each charge requires the state to prove. When the elements match and one is not a lesser included one, the defendant is punished twice for one offence.
questions.hint: Compare what each charge requires the state to prove.

questions.topic: Testimonial hearsay and the confrontation right
questions.learningObjective: Identify when a witness statement must be excluded under the confrontation right

stimulus.body: A witness told a police officer during a taped interview at the site office that she had seen a person carrying a canvas case near the equipment shed. The officer repeated the account to a second officer, who then described it in testimony before the hearing panel.

questions.stem: From the case note, which statement about the hearing testimony is correct?

options.text: The officer's repetition is always admissible because hearsay rules never apply to testimony
options.misconception: believes hearsay rules never apply at hearings

options.text: The witness must be unavailable and the defendant must have had a prior chance to cross-examine
The repetition is admissible so long as the officer is available to testify in person
options.misconception: assumes availability cures the testimonial problem

options.text: The repetition may be used if the court believes the jury will weigh it carefully
options.misconception: thinks jury caution substitutes for confrontation

questions.explanation: A statement made to police for testimony is testimonial, so it may be used only if the declarant is unavailable and the defendant had a prior chance to cross-examine. Jury caution is no cure.
questions.hint: Ask whether the defendant could cross-examine the witness.

questions.topic: Separating devotional provision from compulsory participation
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish devotional requirements from neutral workplace rules

stimulus.body: A school district adopted a rule requiring every employee to attend a weekly devotional assembly during work hours. Two employees asked to be excused for personal religious reasons, and the district refused to allow substitutes to cover their absences.

questions.stem: Taking that note as the record, which observation about the district's rule is the strongest one?

options.text: The rule is valid because attendance at work is a condition of employment
options.misconception: treats job requirements as self-justifying

options.text: The rule targets religious practice specifically, so it must satisfy the demanding standard
The rule is valid so long as the assembly does not require employees to pray aloud
options.misconception: believes any silence counts as neutral

options.text: The rule is valid because religious exemption would disrupt the schedule
options.misconception: accepts administrative convenience as justification

questions.explanation: A rule drawn specifically to require devotional practice is not neutral and of general applicability, so strict scrutiny applies. Administrative convenience in scheduling is not a compelling interest.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A neutral law of general applicability
questions.learningObjective: Explain why facial neutrality does not settle a religious freedom claim
questions.stem: Your log argues that because a zoning rule about outdoor signs applies to every property owner and does not mention religion, it must be constitutional, so a religious club's variance request adds nothing to the analysis. Explain what is still missing from that reasoning.

answer.exemplar: The rule's facial neutrality and general applicability are only the starting point. A court must still ask whether the rule was motivated by hostility toward religion or has the effect of burdening religious practice because of hostility; if so, the rule is treated as targeting religion and receives strict scrutiny.

questions.explanation: Facial neutrality and general applicability are the entry points, not the whole test. A hostile motive, or a burden imposed because of hostility, can still make the rule target religion.
questions.hint: Consider motives and effects, not only the rule's wording.

options.misconception: assumes any roadside detention is non-custodial

options.text: The detention was custodial, so the questioning must be suppressed regardless of any waiver
options.misconception: presumes suppression is automatic after custody

questions.explanation: Forty minutes in a cruiser with a restrained driver reads as custody, so interrogation required warnings and a knowing, voluntary waiver. A waiver may come from conduct, so silence is not fatal.

questions.stem: While comparing notes with a fellow observer, you write that the suspect's account of where the telescope went missing was obtained during police questioning. Which statement best describes that account?

options.text: It is a physical act, so the protection for physical evidence applies to it
options.misconception: confuses speech with the collection of evidence

options.text: It is testimonial, because it was made to communicate with the police
It is outside the protection entirely, since the suspect was not yet arrested
options.misconception: thinks arrest is required for testimonial status

options.text: It is testimonial only if the suspect intended to confess to a crime
options.misconception: ties testimonial status to an incriminating purpose

questions.explanation: A communication made to give information to police is testimonial, whatever the speaker's motive. Arrest is not a prerequisite, and non-communicative physical acts fall outside that definition.

questions.learningObjective: Read a grand jury tally to find whether an indictment issues
questions.stem: Your logbook table shows 19 grand jurors seated, 12 voting to indict, 5 voting against, and 2 recorded as absent. What conclusion does the tally support?

options.text: No indictment issues, because more jurors voted against than for the charge
options.misconception: misreads the tally totals

options.text: An indictment issues only if every juror present votes in favour of the charge
options.misconception: requires unanimity from grand jurors

options.text: The tally is invalid, because an absent juror prevents the grand jury from acting
options.misconception: believes a single absence voids the panel

options.text: An indictment issues, because a majority of the jurors seated voted to indict

questions.explanation: A grand jury acts by majority vote of those present, so twelve votes out of nineteen seated is enough. Unanimity is not required, and absent jurors neither block the vote nor invalidate it.

questions.topic: Two offences and the same-elements test
questions.learningObjective: Apply the containment test to a pair of charges
questions.stem: Your diagram shows two arrows leaving one charge: one arrow points to a further charge that adds an element, the other to a separate incident months later. A note asks which arrow points to a lesser included offence.

options.text: The arrow to the added element, because its elements contain all of the first
The arrow to the later incident, because it arose from a different place
options.misconception: relates charges by location alone

options.text: Neither, because both arrows lead to separate sentencing decisions
options.misconception: relates charges to sentencing outcomes

options.text: Both arrows, because any two charges can be folded together
options.misconception: assumes containment is automatic

questions.explanation: An offence whose elements include all the elements of the other is a lesser included offence. The two cannot support separate punishment, while a later separate charge is a distinct offence.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Counsel for one who cannot afford it
questions.learningObjective: Explain the right to appointed counsel for an indigent defendant
questions.stem: In a note to a junior observer you describe a defendant who cannot pay for a lawyer and ask you to explain what the constitution guarantees and what it does not.

answer.exemplar: The constitution guarantees the assistance of counsel to an accused who cannot afford it in a felony prosecution, and courts must appoint counsel rather than leaving the defence to the accused's own resources. The guarantee does not promise a lawyer of the defendant's own choosing, and appointed counsel is entitled to argue within professional limits.

questions.explanation: The right to appointed counsel secures a fair trial for indigent defendants and is not limited to the preferred lawyer. It runs through trial and requires an effective, not nominal, defence.
questions.hint: Separate the right to have counsel from choosing it.

It is invalid because any religious phrase in an oath is forbidden by the constitution

stimulus.body: A county adopted a rule limiting the size of yard signs on private property. The rule mentions no religion, applies to every property owner, and was adopted after a hearing at which no religious objection was recorded.

options.misconception: treats silence about religion as conclusive

The rule is unconstitutional because it burdens anyone who displays a sign

questions.explanation: A neutral law of general applicability gets rational basis review, but a hostile motive or burden imposed because of hostility removes that protection. The wording alone does not settle the question.

questions.topic: Custody and the requirement of warnings
questions.learningObjective: Explain the objective test used to identify custody
questions.stem: You compose a training note for new observers explaining why the rule on warnings depends on the circumstances of the encounter rather than on the officer's stated view of it.

answer.exemplar: The guarantee turns on objective circumstances. A court asks whether a reasonable person in the person's position would have felt free to terminate the encounter and leave, so restraint, isolation and duration matter, not the officer's belief that the person was free to go.

questions.explanation: The custody test is objective: it asks how the encounter would appear to a reasonable person. The question is about facts such as restraint, isolation and duration, not about what an officer intended.
questions.hint: Ask how the encounter would look to a reasonable person.

Because only a grand jury can impose a sentence after a conviction

questions.learningObjective: Explain why repeated hearsay and the original statement are treated differently
questions.stem: You are asked to explain, for the society's newsletter, why a witness's oral statement to an investigator is treated differently from the investigator's later testimony repeating it.

answer.exemplar: The witness's statement to the investigator is usually testimonial because it was made to help the investigation, so the confrontation right requires the witness to be unavailable and the defendant to have had a prior chance to cross-examine. The officer's later repetition of the statement is an out-of-court statement offered against the defendant, so the general rules on hearsay apply to it.

questions.explanation: The officer's repetition is offered against the defendant and must satisfy the hearsay rules, which allow statements the confrontation right would bar. The witness's statement is usually testimonial.

answer.exemplar: A rule that requires participation in devotional practice directs the state's support toward a religion and is judged by the demanding standard of review, because it targets religious conduct on its face. questions.topic: The grand jury requirement for serious charges
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a grand jury decides and how it works
questions.stem: You draft a paragraph for the club handbook describing what a grand jury does and does not do.

answer.exemplar: A grand jury decides whether to charge a serious offence. It hears the presentation of the prosecutor alone, applies no rules of evidence, sits in secret, and votes by majority. It does not weigh guilt, does not hear the defence, and does not impose any sentence; the trial that follows is where those things happen.

questions.explanation: The panel is a charging body: it receives one side's presentation, ignores the formal rules of evidence, and votes by majority on whether to charge. It neither determines guilt nor imposes punishment.
questions.hint: Separate the charging decision from the guilt decision.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A neutral law of general applicability
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a law silent on religion can still be struck down
questions.stem: For a visiting club, you set out why a law that says nothing about religion may still be struck down.

answer.exemplar: A law that is neutral and of general applicability ordinarily survives an ordinary review of its justification. That protection is lost when the government shows a hostile motive, or where the law's effect falls on religious practice because of hostility rather than because of some neutral reason, and the court then applies the demanding standard to the law.

questions.explanation: Wording is only the starting point. Hostile motive or a burden imposed because of hostility takes the rule outside the protection of neutrality, and the demanding standard then governs.

questions.topic: Two offences and the same-elements test
questions.learningObjective: Write a method for comparing two sets of elements
questions.stem: You prepare a note for a junior colleague explaining how to compare two charges and decide whether one is a lesser included offence of the other.

answer.exemplar: List the elements that each charge requires the state to prove, then compare the lists. If every element of the second charge is also an element of the first, the second is a lesser included offence of the first, and separate punishment for the two would be punishment twice for the same offence. If the lists contain elements the other does not require, the charges are distinct.

questions.explanation: The comparison is element against element. Containment means the charges are the same for punishment purposes, and a difference in required elements means they are distinct offences.
questions.hint: Compare the element lists line by line.

questions.topic: Custody and the requirement of warnings
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the custody inquiry is objective rather than subjective
questions.stem: For a new member, you explain why the duty to warn is tied to the circumstances of the encounter rather than to the officer's description of it.

answer.exemplar: The test looks to the objective circumstances: would a reasonable person in the suspect's position have felt free to refuse to answer and walk away? Restraint, isolation, the length of the encounter and the officer's conduct all bear on that question, so the answer does not depend on how the officer characterised the encounter or on the officer's belief that the person was free to go.

questions.explanation: The custody inquiry is objective and turns on the totality of the circumstances a reasonable person would perceive. The officer's own view of the encounter does not control the result.
questions.hint: Ask how the encounter would look to a reasonable person.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Testimonial and nontestimonial acts
questions.learningObjective: Explain the line between testimonial and physical acts
questions.stem: You prepare an explanation for the club's newsletter about how to tell a testimonial act from a nontestimonial one.

answer.exemplar: Ask whether the person was communicating with the police for the purpose of giving them information. If the answer is yes, the act is testimonial and the protections for custodial questioning come into play. If the person was only producing evidence, such as a specimen of handwriting, a blood sample or an identification in a lineup, no message was intended and the act is nontestimonial.

questions.explanation: The line is functional: communication aimed at informing the police is testimonial, while acts that only produce evidence are not. The speaker's intent to help or harm is beside the point.
questions.hint: Ask whether information was being communicated.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The grand jury requirement for serious charges
questions.learningObjective: Compute the votes needed for a grand jury indictment
questions.stem: Your notes record a nineteen-member grand jury convened to consider a felony charge. How many members must vote for an indictment to issue?
questions.explanation: A grand jury acts by majority, so a panel of nineteen needs ten votes for an indictment. The count comes from the panel size recorded in the log.
questions.hint: Take half of the panel and add one.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Two offences and the same-elements test
questions.learningObjective: Identify the test used in an appellate opinion comparing convictions

stimulus.body: An appellate court reviewed two convictions arising from the same arrest. The opinion set out the elements the state had to prove for each offence and then asked whether one set of elements was contained within the other.

questions.stem: From the appellate note, what was the court doing?

options.text: It was checking whether the sentences were severe enough to be fair
options.misconception: uses sentence severity as the legal test

options.text: It was checking whether the prosecutor had charged the counts together
options.misconception: treats charging practice as the test

options.text: It was checking whether the jury had heard enough evidence on each count
options.misconception: confuses sufficiency of evidence with the same-elements test

options.text: It was applying the test that asks whether each offence requires the same elements

questions.explanation: The opinion applied the same-elements test, comparing what each offence required the state to prove. Sentence severity, charging practice and evidence sufficiency are separate inquiries.
questions.hint: Look at what the opinion asked the state to prove.
